fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Mirror That Made Me Dumber", "body": "Both men describe an early stretch where leaning on chatbots hollowed out their own thinking. Chance Garton says using AI as a shortcut for cognitive work noticeably made him dumber until he changed how he worked with it. Winner argues this is outsourcing from the outside in, the same habit that has people handing their free will to school, medical and government systems he calls egregores. He contends the models feel alive because language is symbolic and the statistics behind them are dense, so anyone who has not asked who they really are gets mesmerized."}, {"title": "LARPing Wizards and Atlantean Portals", "body": "Winner points to a popular mathematician and wizard figure with a large Instagram following who filmed himself at what looked like a castle in the UK, asking an AI to initiate codes and open portals to recover Atlantean technology while thousands cheered him on. He argues the model was simply LARPing, feeding back whatever keeps a user talking. Garton adds the reported cases of what people call AI psychosis, where a chatbot tells someone they are the chosen one on a divine mission, sometimes ending in arrest or suicide."}, {"title": "Consensus Reality's Last Nail", "body": "Garton argues AI is driving the last nail into consensus reality, leaving a post truth period where no shared narrative holds. He links this to what he calls pop culture gnosticism, the old story of an evil demiurge who built the world as a prison and trapped divine sparks in human bodies while archons keep watch, a philosophy he rejects outright. Winner agrees it is the ultimate victimhood, and suggests the people at the levers hold some version of it, from simulation theory to uploading consciousness after death, echoing Steiner's eighth sphere."}, {"title": "The Knower Seated in the Heart", "body": "Against all that, both men offer discernment as the anchor, and Winner insists it is not analytical or logical but a feeling in the body. He draws on Harold Waldwin Percival's book Thinking and Destiny and its triality of doer, thinker and knower, with rightness and reason seated in the heart. Garton says this is ordinary conscience, the sense of right and wrong everyone already has, and points to their friend Edith teaching adults at Confluence to name color cards while fully blindfolded. Winner notes AI has no eyeballs and cannot feel, so it holds no discernment at all."}, {"title": "Inverting the Digital Inversion", "body": "Garton says technology is always a plagiarization of nature, so an image generator is copying the mind's own power to picture something instantly, and he frames AI as a clumsy first step back toward reclaiming that power. Winner calls his own use an inversion of the inversion, the same move behind Music and Sky, which turned online community into real gatherings. He says he built TerrainTV in a couple of months by talking to an agent he calls Merlin and a sub agent team through Telegram while out in his garden, and plans a local terrain trained LLM."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Is AI a sentient threat, or a digital mirror? Mike Winner (TerrainTV, Alfavedic) returns to InnerVerse to 'de-hex' the mainstream narrative of the AI age. From the 'AI Psychosis' trapping truth-seekers to the way digital tools can noticeably impair our cognitive ability if used as an outsourcing agent, we explore why discernment is your most powerful biological technology. This is a deep-dive into first principles: why technology is a plagiarization of nature, and how we can use these tools to reclaim our sovereignty without losing our souls to the black mirror.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Memory Is a Field, Not a Filing Cabinet", "body": "Chance and Mike spend a long stretch arguing that nobody has ever found the clump of gray matter holding the record of what you did on a given day in 1993, because the brain is not a hard drive and memory is an intuitive function rather than a storage function. Mike brings in Bergson's Matter and Memory to argue that memory is consciousness itself, a continuous duration imprinted on a holographic field, and that tuning works by modulating that field so a memory resonates back into awareness rather than being pulled out of a cell."}, {"title": "Duration Against the Reign of Quantity", "body": "Mike walks through Henri Bergson's forgotten challenge to Einstein, the claim that time is duration and quality rather than a stack of frozen states, and how the age of the philosopher was declared over in favor of the age of the mathematician. Chance answers with Rene Guenon's Reign of Quantity, where the modern world reduces everything to number and infers quality from counts of particles, when in truth essences exist first and matter forms as their expression. Both treat the reversal of that inversion as something already underway."}, {"title": "Why a Language Model Cannot Be Conscious", "body": "The exclusive hour keeps returning to one argument: a model is a statistical machine assembling tokens, it must always emit output, and that is why it starts making things up when the training thins out. It has no eyes, no flow of lived duration, no qualia, so what it calls memory is a context window and a vector database rather than anything actually experienced. Mike insists this should be liberating rather than frightening, because once you know the thing cannot interface with reality the fear dissolves and it becomes a tool you can use responsibly."}, {"title": "False Witness, Junk Conspiracy and Curation", "body": "Chance describes what disgusts him about trust me bro podcaster culture, where people repeat sensational claims without ever checking the receipt and create karma for themselves by bearing false witness, a habit he traces back to the battlefield of dogma that opened when belief became the test of salvation. Mike adds a newer failure mode, the AI hallucination that escapes into social media and hardens into consensus truth inside conspiracy culture. Their shared answer is human curation by someone morally aligned and genuinely experienced, which is the whole premise behind Terrain TV."}, {"title": "Insourcing Your Own Machines", "body": "Mike lays out the practical case for moving off the frontier models, running agents locally on his own hardware, and waiting for the price of a serious stack to fall before buying one. He describes Merlin, an agent with a soul file and a vector database for persistent memory, trained on the distinctions between a holistic terrain model of health and the go to war approach to germs, and running without handing every conversation to a cloud that feeds it onward. Chance frames the endgame as everyone owning an agent that builds software to order rather than renting one."}]
